intro: Mahler’s Ninth grows from a broken rhythm and a two-note sigh into an immense first movement. Bruno Walter conducts the Vienna Philharmonic in 1938, in the hall where he gave its première in 1912.

sections.label: A · A broken rhythm becomes a song
sections.mNote: Cellos, horn and harp precede the second violins’ D-major tune

sections.label: B · Violins push into D minor
sections.mNote: A sharper upward melody crosses the opening’s falling phrases

sections.label: Dev · Horns and timpani recall the opening
sections.mNote: Short rhythms emerge from the thinning orchestra

sections.label: Dev · Brass calls against running strings
sections.mNote: The two themes collide in quickening orchestral writing

sections.label: Link · Low strings in the shadows
sections.mNote: Hesitant violin lines climb above the returning low-string figure

sections.label: Link · The opening rhythm in low brass
sections.mNote: Trombones and tuba enlarge the first hesitant notes

sections.label: A′ · The D-major song returns
sections.mNote: Harp and plucked basses recover the opening’s steadier pulse

sections.label: Coda · Horn, harp and scattered replies
sections.mNote: The orchestra thins to solo lines and a final D

cues.title: A rhythm finding its feet
cues.text: Cellos begin a halting rhythm and a horn completes it. The harp answers with firmer steps, then another horn tries a little melody. Mahler starts with separate voices, each leaving room for the next.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition first-edition score, 1912, p. 1. Lew Smoley describes the successive cello, horn and harp figures: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-1-andante-comodo/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two notes become a song
cues.text: The second violins take a falling second — just two neighbouring notes — and grow a D-major tune from it. Divided violas rock underneath. The melody keeps coming back to that small downward sigh.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 1–2; Smoley identifies the second-violin melody, falling seconds and rocking viola accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Walter returns to the Musikverein
cues.text: Vienna, 16 January 1938. Bruno Walter stands before the orchestra that gave the Ninth its première under him in June 1912, in this same Musikverein hall. Mahler never heard the symphony; he died a year before that first performance.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding, Library of Congress essay, pp. 1–2, on the première, recording and shared venue. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: D major turns minor
cues.text: D minor darkens the music. First violins push upwards in angular phrases, leaning on weak beats; pieces of the gentler tune fall around them. The two melodies pull in opposite directions.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s first-movement guide describes the D-minor second subject, its upward contour and offbeat accents, with fragments of the first subject alongside it.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The horns remember
cues.text: The orchestra subsides to a timpani roll. Four horns bring back the broken rhythm from the opening; the timpani answer with the steadier one. Low winds and strings pick up the scraps in the uneasy country between B♭ major and G minor.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s guide, beginning of the development: diminishing timpani roll, four horns, answering timpani and the B♭-major/G-minor setting.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two machines beside the timpani
cues.text: Producer Fred Gaisberg sits near the timpani, facing Walter. Two machines take turns cutting the performance into wax: one records while the other is reloaded. Beside the engineer, a musician follows the full score, keeping the joins clear of the music’s path.
cues.evidence: Gaisberg’s account of the 1938 session, quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay, p. 2. It describes his seat, the alternating wax-disc machines and the musician following the score.

cues.title: Strings in the shadows
cues.text: Low strings begin their rocking figure again, barely stirring. Above them the violins climb by semitones, one group following another. Horns repeat the little falling sigh as the D-major melody slowly finds its way back.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the shadowy passage after the central conflict: low-string figures, successive chromatic violin ascents, horn seconds and recovery of D major.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The small rhythm becomes enormous
cues.text: Trombones and tuba thunder out the hesitant rhythm that began the symphony. The running notes fall away around it. Timpani, plucked basses and muted violins are left to answer in fragments.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s guide identifies the enlarged opening rhythm in low brass at the great climax, followed by timpani, pizzicato basses and muted violin fragments.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A horn opens the coda
cues.text: A horn lifts the minor third back into D major. Harp arpeggios rise beneath a held wind chord, and the horn continues a long phrase over rocking cellos. The orchestra is becoming a handful of players.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, closing pages, pp. 56–58; Smoley describes the horn’s change from minor to major and the harp, winds and cello accompaniment at the coda.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One D left ringing
cues.text: The closing melody passes to a solo violin. Clarinets and horns answer with falling seconds; the harp climbs through a D-major chord. At the end, a plucked note catches the light of a held D in piccolo and cello.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, final pages of movement I; Smoley identifies the solo violin, repeated falling seconds, harp ascent and final D in piccolo and cello.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The horn’s sigh turns dark
transitions.from: A · A broken rhythm becomes a song
transitions.to: B · Violins push into D minor
transitions.how: The horn repeats the falling second as the harmony turns to D minor. Cellos add rising triplets; first violins press into the sharper second theme on a weak beat. Falling phrases from the first tune remain in the accompanying parts.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s first-movement guide, transition from the D-major first subject to the D-minor second subject.

transitions.title: A B♭ chord leaves a timpani roll
transitions.from: B · Violins push into D minor
transitions.to: Dev · Horns and timpani recall the opening
transitions.how: The exposition reaches a B♭-major chord with an added sixth. A timpani roll survives it and fades. Four horns recover the opening’s broken rhythm, then the timpani answer with the other opening figure as the harmony moves between B♭ and G minor.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the closing B♭ chord, lingering timpani roll and first exchanges of the development.

transitions.title: Trumpet calls set the strings running
transitions.from: Dev · Horns and timpani recall the opening
transitions.to: Dev · Brass calls against running strings
transitions.how: Muted trumpet tattoos pass to the timpani as the orchestra grows. Winds and stopped horns sound the rising call; low winds and strings answer with descending chromatic notes. The pace quickens, with triplets crossing the strings’ semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide, approach to the faster central development and its opposing brass, wind and string figures.

transitions.title: The low strings begin again
transitions.from: Dev · Brass calls against running strings
transitions.to: Link · Low strings in the shadows
transitions.how: The short descending phrases dwindle into a pause. Low strings quietly restart the rocking figure; first and second violins climb by semitones in overlapping lines. Horns keep repeating a falling minor second until D major begins to emerge.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the silence, low-string restart and chromatic violin ascents in the shadowy passage.

transitions.title: The opening rhythm in trombones and tuba
transitions.from: Link · Low strings in the shadows
transitions.to: Link · The opening rhythm in low brass
transitions.how: Rushing orchestral lines plunge downwards. Through them, trombones and tuba hammer an enlarged version of the first cello-and-horn rhythm. The rapid notes die away, leaving timpani blows and the low brass to repeat the opening figures.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide, climax at the end of the development and its low-brass and timpani aftermath.

transitions.title: Harp and basses recover the pulse
transitions.from: Link · The opening rhythm in low brass
transitions.how: A muted trumpet call accompanies the cadence into D major. Harp and plucked low strings recover the steadier opening rhythm. Horns continue the first theme, with clarinets and shimmering violins moving beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the return to D major after the march-like aftermath, with muted trumpet, harp, pizzicato basses, horns and clarinets.

transitions.title: The horn raises the third
transitions.to: Coda · Horn, harp and scattered replies
transitions.how: The rising string fragments disappear in D minor. A horn raises the third by a semitone, restoring D major. Harp arpeggios and a sustained wind chord open the coda, with the horn’s long phrase above rocking cello triplets.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 56–58; Smoley identifies the raised third and the coda’s harp, winds and cellos.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement I, printed pp. 1–58: cello, horn and harp opening; second-violin first theme; low-brass climax; horn, harp and solo violin in the coda.

timeline.note: Cellos begin the hesitant rhythm and the fourth horn completes it.
Harp notes and horn calls sound above the violas’ rocking thirds.
Second violins grow their melody from a falling second above divided strings.
First violins push upwards with the sharper D-minor theme.
Horns and timpani recover the opening rhythms among low winds and strings.
Trombones and tuba enlarge the opening rhythm above the rushing strings.
A long horn phrase unfolds over held winds, harp arpeggios and rocking cellos.
Flute and solo violin carry exposed lines between quiet wind and harp replies.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Commons, the surviving concert-programme catalogue and the Library of Congress essay agree on orchestra and conductor.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The recording sources identify the complete movement but do not establish the performing edition or any local alterations. The 1912 full score is used as a structural reference, not proof of the parts on the 1938 desks.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: 16 January is the documented public concert date. Pristine gives 15–16 January 1938 for its reissue; the inspected evidence does not establish whether any rehearsal material entered the issued matrices. The Commons embedded “1962” digitising tag is not accepted as a performance or transfer date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The concert-programme catalogue names the hall and city; Commons uses Musikvereinsaal de Vienne.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names only an unspecified audio CD. HMV made the original 78-rpm issue, but the CD label used for this upload has not been identified.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The source CD catalogue number is unknown. Pristine documents the historical ten-disc HMV set as DB 8569–8578; that does not identify the carrier transferred for Commons.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Pristine lists the original complete-set matrix series 2VH 7027–7046. The inspected DAHR composer listing did not establish a matrix/take match for this digital source; no exhaustive absence is claimed. Specific takes and a verified movement-to-matrix mapping remain unestablished, so the complete-set series is not presented as a side identification for this file.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No engineer for the source CD or Commons transfer is identified. Gaisberg was the original recording producer and Charlie Gregory the recording engineer, not established digital-transfer credits. Andrew Rose’s named 2013 Pristine transfer is a different reissue and is not the source of this Commons upload.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The embedded digitising value 1962 is not corroborated as a transfer date and is not used as one; neither upload nor release dates substitute for it.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Commons supplies an Ogg Vorbis file and an MP3 access derivative.
fields.note: Embedded metadata names Xiph.Org libVorbis I 20100325 (Everywhere). The original 1938 performance was cut on alternating wax-recording machines, but the intervening CD restoration, equalisation, edits and mastering are not identified for this file.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: The underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mahler died in 1911. This is a term calculation for the composition, not worldwide clearance of an unidentified edition or transfer.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the sound recording.
fields.note: The inspected template expressly concerns expired performer and producer rights in the European Union. This package is admitted on that territorial recording-rights basis, not merely the composition’s age. United States status is not established; no worldwide public-domain clearance is asserted.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
